profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the backend platform team and the developer productivity team at a fintech company building a mobile payment product. The company is launching a six-week Kanban pilot on the checkout backend team and wants lightweight workflow telemetry added to existing engineering tools so internal process researchers can study how Kanban affects communication and collaboration without interrupting delivery. The immediate purpose of the meeting is to align on the telemetry interface, what state the handoff must be in before the pilot starts, how to backfill the board history for comparison, and how schema changes will be handled if the workflow evolves mid-pilot. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the integration plan, timing, and maintenance responsibilities for the telemetry handoff.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: service integration, event-driven systems, Jira automation, delivery planning for payments infrastructure
members.background: Nina leads the backend team responsible for checkout and settlement services in the mobile payment stack. Her team recently shifted from sprint-based planning to a Kanban-style flow in a newly created Jira project, and she is coordinating several low-risk process changes while protecting delivery commitments.
members.private_state: Nina wants the telemetry work to remain lightweight and strictly bounded so it does not disrupt the pilot or create an open-ended maintenance obligation for her team.
hidden_assumptions: If a feed is described as ready for consumption, that normally means producers have published stable events to the agreed topic or webhook endpoint so downstream teams can start consuming when they are ready.
The board for this pilot naturally refers to her team's new Jira Kanban board in the pilot project, because that is the operational board the team is actually using day to day.
Backfilling the board history means replaying whatever issue transition history exists for that current Kanban board, not reconstructing workflow equivalents from earlier sprint artifacts.
When someone says we will manage schema updates, the shared analytics or platform-owning side usually handles the canonical schema while her team only reports local workflow changes.
A coordination meeting about telemetry handoff usually settles interface and timing, not long-term ownership details unless someone explicitly raises them.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: engineering analytics, workflow instrumentation, internal research tooling, cross-team coordination
members.background: Leo manages internal developer productivity tooling used to study delivery patterns and collaboration across engineering teams. He works with process researchers who combine Jira workflow data, pull request metadata, and deployment signals into standardized dashboards intended to compare teams over time.
members.private_state: Leo needs this pilot to produce analytically usable, comparable data from day one and hopes the backend team will absorb more of the workflow-specific upkeep than they explicitly negotiate.
hidden_assumptions: If a telemetry handoff is described as ready for consumption, that means the data is already flowing through the analytics pipeline in a usable form and can be consumed by dashboards and researchers without extra producer-side rework.
The board in a Kanban study refers to the standardized workflow board model used by the research tooling, even if the source team has its own local Jira board underneath.
Backfilling the board history means reconstructing the team's immediately preceding workflow timeline so the pilot can be compared to what the team was doing right before the Kanban switch.
When someone says we will manage schema updates, the producing workflow owners are implicitly included because only they can keep mappings accurate when statuses or automation rules change.
Comparability across the full six-week study requires continuity across board changes unless someone explicitly excludes the pre-pilot period.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the telemetry should be ready for consumption by next Wednesday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means the backend team will have stable event payloads emitted from staging into the agreed topic, with field names settled enough that downstream consumers can begin integrating.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means the telemetry will already be flowing end-to-end through the shared analytics pipeline, validated for completeness, and visible in the standard dashboard for researchers to use.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Ready for consumption sounds like a routine coordination milestone and is more naturally ambiguous than simply saying ready; both hear it as a practical handoff phrase used all the time between producer and consumer teams, so neither expects it to hide different completion standards.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss capturing transitions from the board and aligning the board states.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina is referring to her team's newly created Jira Kanban board for the checkout backend pilot, including its local columns and automation rules.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo is referring to the standardized cross-team board model used by the research tooling, which maps multiple Jira workflows into a common lane structure for comparison.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both objects are legitimately called the board in this organization, and because the meeting is explicitly about Kanban telemetry, the phrase feels fully grounded without either person realizing the other is picturing a different board artifact.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'backfill the board history'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to backfill the board history before the pilot starts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina assumes this means replaying the available status-change history from the current Kanban board so the initial charts are not empty when the pilot begins.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo assumes this includes reconstructing the team's immediately prior workflow history from the old sprint board or equivalent issue states so researchers can compare pre-pilot and early-pilot behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase board history sounds specific enough to feel clarified already, but its boundary is left implicit; each person applies the obvious scope from their own work context, and the overlap with the term board further masks the difference.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included in 'we will manage schema updates'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They say that if statuses change during the pilot, we will manage schema updates.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina presupposes we refers mainly to the shared analytics side maintaining the canonical schema and mappings, with her team notifying them when workflow statuses change.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo presupposes we includes Nina's team as the practical owner of updating mappings and version details because they control the workflow and produce the events.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The collective we sounds cooperative and responsible, which reduces pressure to assign a named owner in the moment; both think they have acknowledged the issue, while each silently projects their organization's usual ownership convention onto the same sentence.

turns.inner_thought: I want to lock this down before the ask grows legs. My team can expose lightweight workflow telemetry from the checkout backend team's current Jira Kanban board, but I do not want this meeting to turn into a broader ownership discussion or an open-ended analytics commitment.
turns.utterance: Thanks for jumping on. We're about to start the six-week Kanban pilot on the checkout backend side, and before my team begins implementation, I want to make sure we're aligned on what telemetry your tooling needs.

turns.inner_thought: What matters is getting analytically usable signals from day one. For the study, we need transitions from the standardized board model, aging signals, and continuity that lets researchers compare the pilot against the team's immediately prior workflow period.
turns.utterance: From our side, the priority is the coordination signals we'd expect Kanban to affect most. So the main pieces are capturing transitions from the board, card aging, and enough continuity that the study has a usable baseline.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds manageable. The team's new Jira Kanban board in the pilot project already emits status-change webhooks, so instrumenting that board should be simple and nicely bounded.
turns.utterance: That part should be straightforward. We already have status-change webhooks coming off the board, so capturing transitions there shouldn't take much extra work.

turns.inner_thought: As long as their local workflow maps cleanly into our standard research board model, we can keep the metrics comparable with other teams. I don't need to get into the model details unless they ask.
turns.utterance: Great. As long as we align the board states, that should fit cleanly with what we're already using on the analytics side.

turns.inner_thought: I can commit to stable staging events by next Wednesday if we freeze the payload shape in the next few days. For me, ready for consumption means published payloads on the agreed interface so downstream teams can start integrating when they're ready.
turns.utterance: On timing, I think we can have the telemetry ready for consumption by next Wednesday, assuming we lock the payload shape over the next couple of days.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. If it's ready for consumption by next Wednesday, I can count on it being usable through the analytics pipeline without more producer-side churn. That's what the researchers need for a clean start.
turns.utterance: Next Wednesday works for us. Once it's ready for consumption, it can flow right into our pipeline.

turns.inner_thought: I can replay whatever transition history exists for the current Kanban board so the initial charts aren't empty when the pilot begins. That gives them something to look at without reopening old sprint artifacts.
turns.utterance: I can also backfill the board history before the pilot starts so the first charts aren't empty on day one.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Backfilling the board history should cover the continuity we need, including the workflow period right before the Kanban switch, so the study has a real baseline instead of starting cold.
turns.utterance: Yes, that would help a lot. Backfilling the board history should give us the baseline we need for the study.

turns.inner_thought: I should flag that statuses may shift, but without volunteering my team for ongoing schema maintenance. If we rename columns or add something like Blocked, we'll send the updated values and the analytics side can take care of the canonical schema work.
turns.utterance: One thing to note: if we tweak column names or add a blocked state mid-pilot, I can send over the updated values and schema updates will be managed.

turns.inner_thought: That's acceptable, and in practice it means their team will help keep the mappings accurate because they control the live workflow. We'll support, but I expect the workflow owners to absorb most of that upkeep as changes happen.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine. Since the workflow owners will usually spot status changes first, schema updates will be managed as the pilot evolves.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, this seems settled: capture transitions from our current Jira Kanban board, replay its existing history, and have stable event payloads ready by next Wednesday. That's contained and shouldn't create a lasting maintenance burden for my team.
turns.utterance: Alright, then from my side the plan is: we'll capture transitions from the board, backfill the board history, and have the feed ready for consumption by next Wednesday.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If the data lands end to end, includes the continuity I expect, and the producing team helps keep mappings current, the study should launch cleanly and we won't need another negotiation unless something major changes.
turns.utterance: That should give the study a clean start, and any minor schema changes can be handled as they come up.
